strengths: Pioneering and highly valuable contribution that introduces the first large-scale RGB-Thermal (RGBT) visual grounding benchmark (RGBT-GroundBench), filling a crucial gap for robust language-guided perception in adverse real-world environments.

Comprehensive and rich multi-level annotations covering scene types, environmental conditions (weather and illumination), and object properties (size and occlusion), which enables systematic and fine-grained robustness diagnostics.

Well-designed and effective reference baseline (RGBT-VGNet) featuring Asymmetric Modality Adaptation (AMA) to balance pretrained modality bias, and Tri-Prior Fusion (TPF) for adaptive illumination-aware integration.

Exceptionally rigorous and thorough evaluation that benchmarks 11 representative grounding methods and several state-of-the-art multimodal large language models (MLLMs) under a unified protocol, deriving deep scientific insights into cross-spectral reasoning.
Exemplary commitment to reproducibility and open-source science by releasing code, annotations, checkpoints, and evaluation scripts.
weaknesses: The benchmark is constructed from existing RGBT object detection datasets (FLIR, M3FD, MFAD) rather than newly captured raw footage, meaning the visual diversity and scene distributions are fundamentally bounded by these underlying source datasets.

The baseline method (RGBT-VGNet) relies on relatively standard components (asymmetric LoRA ranks, cross-attention, and heuristic weight calculation), representing incremental algorithmic novelty, though it serves exceptionally well as a solid, reproducible reference point.

The dataset curation depends heavily on Qwen3-VL auto-captioning, and while a rigorous hierarchical random sampling was applied for quality control, only 15% of the instances were manually reviewed, leaving a potential for minor residual label noise in the unreviewed subset.

strengths: First large-scale benchmark for RGB-Thermal (TIR) 2D visual grounding, addressing a critical gap where RGB-only models fail under adverse conditions like low illumination and foggy weather.

Comprehensive and fine-grained annotations covering 13 scene types, 4 weather categories, 4 illumination levels, as well as occlusion and scale attributes, which allow for systematic diagnostic evaluations.

Establishment of a unified evaluation protocol adapting 11 representative visual grounding models (RGB-only, TIR-only, and multi-modal) under a shared code base, ensuring fair and reproducible comparisons.

A well-designed reference baseline (RGBT-VGNet) featuring Asymmetric Modality Adaptation (AMA), Language-Aware Visual Synergy (LAVS), and Tri-Prior Fusion (TPF), which consistently outperforms prior methods.

Extensive experimental evaluations, including diagnostic subset breakdowns, evaluations with stricter IoU thresholds (Acc@0.7), and benchmarking of state-of-the-art Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs).
weaknesses: The visual data is derived entirely from pre-existing object detection datasets (FLIR, M3FD, MFAD) rather than newly collected real-world imagery, which slightly limits the absolute novelty of the raw sensor data.

The initial referring expressions are synthesized using Qwen3-VL, which may introduce systematic language patterns or biases inherent to the generator model, even though human verification and quality control were applied.

Lack of technical details regarding how weak spatial alignment (frequent in FLIR/M3FD due to parallax or differing optical centers) is handled, such as whether separate bounding boxes are maintained for RGB and TIR or if single shared coordinates are assumed.

strengths: Pioneering Benchmark: Introduces RGBT-GroundBench, a timely and large-scale benchmark for RGB-Thermal (TIR) visual grounding, bridging the gap between multi-spectral perception and vision-language tasks.

Unified Codebase and Protocols: Adapts and evaluates 11 representative visual grounding models under a single codebase and unified evaluation protocol, facilitating fair comparisons and future research.

Multi-level Fine-Grained Annotations: Detailed annotations across 13 scene types, 4 weather conditions, 4 illumination levels, occlusion levels, and size groups allow for systematic diagnostics of model failures.
Comprehensive Evaluation: Provides extensive experiments including zero-shot transfer, in-domain training, multi-modal settings, MLLM evaluations, and stricter thresholds (Acc@0.7).
weaknesses: Critical Design Choice (Lack of Disambiguation): In Section 3.2, the authors state: 'we further select the largest instance of each object category per image pair to enhance annotation clarity'. This choice is highly problematic for a visual grounding (referring expression comprehension) dataset. Grounding inherently relies on same-category distractors to test fine-grained disambiguation (e.g., distinguishing between multiple cars or pedestrians). By only annotating the largest instance of each category per image, the task is significantly simplified and leans closer to language-guided category detection rather than true referring expression disambiguation.

Data Novelty & Heritage: The visual data is sourced entirely from existing RGBT object detection datasets (FLIR, M3FD, MFAD). While converting detection datasets to grounding datasets is standard practice, the paper should more clearly delineate the boundaries of its contribution versus the original datasets, especially regarding alignment and image pair selection.

Heavy Reliance on MLLMs for Ground-Truth Annotation: The referring expressions and attribute labels are primarily generated by Qwen3-VL. Although hierarchical random sampling is applied for human verification, the review rate is relatively low (only 15% of instances reviewed, with 5% edited). Given the known hallucination and style biases of MLLMs, this low human-in-the-loop ratio might introduce synthetic biases into the dataset.

Marginal Improvements on Certain Splits: Although RGBT-VGNet performs well overall, the improvement margins over strong multi-modal baselines (such as MV-HiVG) are quite small on several splits, such as RefMFAD (e.g., only 0.52% improvement on the test set under the Acc@0.7 metric in Table 7), indicating limited effectiveness of the custom modules under certain cross-spectral conditions.

strengths: Presents the first large-scale visual grounding benchmark (RGBT-Ground) tailored for complex real-world scenarios using aligned RGB and Thermal infrared (TIR) images.

Provides highly comprehensive and fine-grained annotations across three levels: scene-level (13 categories), environment-level (4 lighting and 4 weather conditions), and object-level (occlusion and size), allowing for rigorous diagnostic analysis of model robustness.
Develops a unified evaluation framework (RGBT-VG) that adapts six classical visual grounding algorithms to support multimodal (RGB-TIR) inputs, creating a standardized testbed for future research.

The proposed baseline, RGBT-VGNet, is technically sound and achieves superior performance by employing well-motivated modules: Asymmetric Modality Adaptation (AMA) to bridge the RGB-TIR domain gap and Language-Aware Visual Synergy (LAVS) to guide fusion with textual semantics.
Includes an exceptionally thorough appendix with extensive experiments, detailed scene/weather/illumination-wise breakdowns, qualitative comparisons, and ablation studies.
weaknesses: The visual imagery in the benchmark is entirely sourced from pre-existing RGBT object detection datasets (FLIR, M3FD, and MFAD). While the referring expressions and multi-level attributes are new, the visual diversity is bounded by these existing domains.

The dataset annotations are initially generated using Qwen-VL. Although the authors mention using a hierarchical random sampling strategy for human verification, the manuscript lacks details on the exact scale of human intervention (e.g., what percentage of the 38,760 expressions were manually corrected) and quality control statistics.

The experiments are conducted at a relatively low resolution of 224x224. Since small objects (occupying less than 1% of the image) represent a significant portion of the dataset (57.7%), this low resolution might create an artificial bottleneck for visual localization compared to native resolutions (640x512).

strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and underserved task in visual grounding (VG): robust localization in complex real-world environments (e.g., night, fog, rain) where standard RGB sensors fail. Proposing an RGBT (RGB + Thermal) benchmark is a timely contribution.

The RGBT-Ground benchmark is richly annotated with hierarchical metadata at the scene-level (13 categories), environment-level (4 weathers, 4 illuminations), and object-level (size, occlusion). This allows for fine-grained diagnostic evaluation.

Instead of just presenting a single new method, the authors build a unified evaluation framework (RGBT-VG) by systematically adapting seven representative RGB-based visual grounding methods to the multimodal setting, facilitating fair comparison.

The proposed RGBT-VGNet baseline is well-motivated, using Asymmetric Modality Adaptation (AMA) via LoRA to bridge the domain gap and Language-Aware Visual Synergy (LAVS) to guide visual fusion with language queries.

The experimental evaluation is highly comprehensive, spanning zero-shot and fully trained settings across three sub-datasets. The appendix provides extensive and meticulous analysis of all 13 scenes, 4 weather conditions, and 4 illumination types.
weaknesses: The visual imagery itself is not newly collected, as it is constructed by aggregating existing RGBT object detection datasets (FLIR, M3FD, MFAD).

The referring expressions are automatically generated using Qwen-VL. Although a random sampling human verification is mentioned, the exact scale and protocol of human cleaning are not fully detailed. Clarifying the percentage of manually verified annotations and the estimated noise rate would improve trust in the benchmark quality.

The algorithmic novelty of RGBT-VGNet is somewhat incremental, as it combines standard techniques like LoRA fine-tuning and cross-attention modules with minor adaptations for asymmetry and text-guidance.

strengths: Introduces RGBT-Ground, the first large-scale benchmark for RGB-Thermal (RGBT) visual grounding, filling an important gap in robust vision-language understanding under challenging conditions like nighttime and adverse weather.

Provides high-quality and comprehensive multi-level annotations encompassing scene-level, environment-level, and object-level attributes, along with rich and diverse referring expressions (average query length of 14.24 words).

Establishes RGBT-VG, a highly valuable unified evaluation framework that standardizes and adapts seven representative visual grounding models to multi-modal visual inputs, facilitating fair comparison and future research.
The proposed RGBT-VGNet baseline is technically sound, effectively addressing the cross-modal domain gap using Asymmetric Modality Adaptation (AMA) and cross-modal fusion guided by language (LAVS).

Presents exceptionally thorough experimental evaluations and ablation studies across three distinct sub-datasets, with extensive fine-grained performance breakdowns across 25+ subsets provided in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: The visual imagery is sourced from pre-existing RGBT object detection datasets (FLIR, M3FD, MFAD) rather than being newly captured, which slightly limits the originality of the raw sensor data.

The referring expressions and environmental annotations are heavily reliant on Qwen-VL API generation in the initial stage. Although human verification was applied, automated generation can still inherit potential biases or subtle errors from the underlying large vision-language model.
A detailed analysis of parameter and computational overhead comparing the proposed asymmetric LoRA adaptation (AMA) with symmetric LoRA or simpler prompt-tuning mechanisms is missing.
